title: Zhukov strikes back at Moscow

facts.text: Late on 29 November 1941, General Georgy Zhukov, commanding the Western Front, assured Stalin that the Germans would not commit large new forces soon. Stalin then handed him three reserve armies, the 1st Shock, 10th and 20th, for a counterattack.
Zhukov says he told Stalin that night that the Germans were "bled white." His plan, sent the next morning, was to strike north and south of Moscow while the enemy was still attacking.

It was a gamble. The US Army history calls the plan a near to last move in a battle that was likely to turn against the Soviets. The acting chief of the General Staff, General Aleksandr Vasilevsky, warned: "If we do not do that in the next few days, it will be too late."

Fresh troops made it possible. By 1 December the Stavka had brought 70 divisions from the Soviet Far East and 27 more from Central Asia and the Transcaucasus, at least 30 percent of the strategic reserves it committed in 1941.

The US Army history credits the spy Richard Sorge, whose reports from Tokyo that Japan would not attack let Moscow risk stripping the east. Soviet codebreakers were also reading Japanese diplomatic messages, so how much rested on Sorge is still debated.

The Kalinin Front went first, on 5 December. In paralyzing morning cold the 29th Army attacked across the frozen Volga west of Kalinin and broke about a mile into the German line. Its front commander, General Ivan Konev, had argued that he lacked the tanks and infantry for it.

Zhukov's Western Front armies joined in on 6 December, as the dawn temperature fell as low as 38 below zero Fahrenheit. The 30th Army broke eight miles into the deep flank of the German Third Panzer Group northeast of Klin.
The Soviets took Solnechnogorsk on 12 December and Klin on 15 December. By 16 December the German spearheads that had been aimed at Moscow were gone.

That day Hitler forbade any large withdrawals, and on 18 December his order demanding "fanatical resistance" reached Army Group Centre. On 19 December he accepted the resignation of the army's commander in chief, Field Marshal Walther von Brauchitsch, and took command of the army himself.
By early January 1942 the Germans had been driven back 100 to 250 km (about 60 to 150 miles) from Moscow. It ended German hopes of a quick victory over the Soviet Union.

declassified.fact: Early in 1942, too late to matter, German intelligence circulated what it said was a transcript of Zhukov and Marshal Semyon Timoshenko urging the Moscow counteroffensive. Timoshenko supposedly predicted that German tanks and motorized artillery would become useless at 20 below zero Fahrenheit, and Zhukov proposed to let the weather decide when to start.

film.license: U.S. government film (War Department); the combat film inside is Soviet newsreel film used by the U.S. film. NARA marks it Restricted Possibly as a blanket note; earlier cards used reels 8 and 10 the same way.
film.shot_notes: Whole reel 6, 8 min 26 s, HD scan; narration and score throughout, so run silent. 00:00 to 00:50 titles (avoid), 01:00 map, 01:30 Stalin quote card, 02:00 to 02:55 Christmas church service and title cards (avoid). NOON: 03:00 to 04:05: ski troops in white advancing in a column (03:00), troops in white with a tank (03:10), artillery firing (03:20, open here on the muzzle blast), troops in the snowy woods (03:30), a fighter low over the snow (03:40), a cavalry charge across the snow (03:50), a shell burst (04:00). 7 P.M. SECOND CUT: 04:10 to 05:58: aircraft over the snow (04:10), ski troops dragging equipment (04:20), a T-34 charging through snow (04:30), shell bursts and explosions (04:40 to 05:10), infantry running forward through the snow (05:50). Open on the T-34 at 04:30. No shot shared with noon. 06:00 to 07:50 liberated towns (Volokolamsk sign at 06:00, Borodino at 07:20) and townspeople; a possible extra for the 7 p.m. cut if needed, avoiding the somber finds in reel 7.

body:
General Ivan Konev argued that he lacked the tanks and infantry to attack. On this morning his armies attacked anyway, across the frozen Volga.

5 December 1941. The Kalinin Front opened the Soviet counteroffensive before Moscow. In paralyzing cold the 29th Army crossed the Volga ice west of Kalinin and broke about a mile into the German line. Zhukov's Western Front joined in the next day.

A week earlier Stalin had handed Zhukov three reserve armies. Divisions from the Far East and Central Asia made it possible, and the spy Richard Sorge's reports that Japan would not attack helped Moscow risk stripping the east, though how much rested on him is still debated.

"If we do not do that in the next few days, it will be too late," General Aleksandr Vasilevsky had warned.

Klin fell on 15 December. On 19 December Hitler took command of the army himself. By early January the Germans had been pushed back 100 to 250 km from Moscow, and their hopes of a quick victory in the east were over.
